country.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/8] Given that the diversity of identity formation can be understood within the context of prolonged adolescence in Japan (Arnett et al., 2014), two different types of identity trajectories could be identi- [/page/3/Text/9] fied, namely, stable identity trajectories and transitional identity trajectories. Following the literature on identity development in Western and Japanese adolescents (e.g., Hatano et al., 2016; Luyckx, Schwartz, Berzonsky, et al., 2008), we hypothesized that five identity trajectories would be identified (similar to those in Luyckx et al., 2013): achievement, foreclosure, moratorium, troubled diffusion, and carefree diffusion. ... The majority of adolescents in contemporary Japan enroll in postsecondary education (i.e., university and vocational school), suggesting that they are exposed to relatively modest environmental changes in adolescence than in young adulthood. In this situation, many Japanese adolescents may tend to be unmotivated to explore their identity issues (i.e., carefree diffusion). [/page/3/Text/10] In addition to these stable trajectories, we hypothesized that a transitional identity trajectory would be identified, specifically, a trajectory from moratorium to achievement. This hypothesis reflects the Japanese context; specifically, the effect of passing through adolescence in a society that is rapidly changing toward valuing individualism (Côté et al., 2016; Sugimura & Mizokami, 2012; Sugimura et al., 2016). This is in line with the argument that identity status does not radically transit toward achievement, but takes a progressive orientation during adolescence (i.e., at least one progressive orientation), based on findings from Western individualistic adolescents (Meeus et al., 2010). Furthermore, crosssectional research indicates that Japanese late adolescents are more inclined toward the achievement classification, and less toward the moratorium classification, compared with early and middle adolescents (Hatano et al., 2016).
